In brief

  • This page lists every hadith on Laylat al-Qadr that the guide cites, with its narrator, collection, number, grading and a link to the source.
  • The Qurʾān gives the night its name in Sūrat al-Qadr and calls it a blessed night in Sūrat al-Dukhān 44:3–4.
  • A narration enters the guide only after its collection, number, wording and grading have been matched in live sources. Anything that cannot be matched is marked NOT_FOUND and held back.
  • Several reports that circulate widely, such as a mild night or sea water turning fresh, are held back for that reason.

Every page of this guide rests on two kinds of evidence: the Qurʾān and the hadith, the recorded sayings and practice of the Prophet ﷺ. This page gathers both in one place. It lists each hadith on Laylat al-Qadr (لَيْلَةُ الْقَدْر, “the Night of Decree”) that the guide relies on, states where it can be found, and explains how each one was checked before it was cited.

The page serves two kinds of reader. A believer preparing for the last ten nights can see at a glance what the Prophet ﷺ said about the night and how strongly each report is attested. A reader who wants to test the guide can follow every link to the source and compare the wording for himself. Where the sources differ on a grading or a translation, the difference is stated openly.

The Qurʾānic sources

The Qurʾān is the first source on the night. A whole chapter carries its name and describes it in five verses: the Qurʾān was sent down on it, it is better than a thousand months, the angels and the Spirit descend in it, and it is peace until dawn. The page on Sūrat al-Qadr explains each verse in turn.

A second passage describes the same night in different words. It calls the night blessed and adds that every wise matter is made distinct in it, which is the sense of “decree” that the name carries. Read with the verse that places the sending down of the Qurʾān in the month of Ramadan, it fixes the night within that month.

The main narrations

The table lists the narrations already cited across this guide. Each row gives a short paraphrase, the Companion who narrated it, the collection and number, the grading, and a link to the report on sunnah.com. The reports in the collections of al-Bukhārī and Muslim carry no separate grading on that site, because both compilers admitted only narrations they judged sound; they are marked “ṣaḥīḥ (collection)”. For the other collections the grading is the one the source displays, with the scholar or edition that issued it.

One narration stands at the head of the list because it states the reward plainly. Its wording ties the forgiveness to the act of standing in prayer and to the intention behind it, and it sets no condition of knowing which night it was:

The reports on the date are best read together, as the page on when Laylat al-Qadr falls does. The reports on the sun, the moon and the rain are set out with their limits on the page on the signs of the night, and the two wordings of the supplication are compared on the duʿāʾ page.

Further narrations

The guide also draws on other authentic narrations that are well known in the literature on the night. Several of them are parallel versions of reports in the first table, transmitted through a different chain and preserved in a different collection. Parallel chains matter because a report that reaches the compilers by more than one route is harder to dismiss as the error of a single transmitter.

Two features of these reports deserve care. The first is counting. The report of ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit says only “the ninth, the seventh and the fifth”, and the English translation supplies the 29th, 27th and 25th. The report of Ibn ʿAbbās counts the same numbers as nights that remain, so the figures can be read from the end of the month. This guide gives the wording as it stands and leaves the counting to the page on the date.

The second is translation. The English rendering of Muslim no. 1166 on sunnah.com says “the last week”, while the Arabic says “the remaining ten”. The paraphrase above follows the Arabic. Where an English translation and its Arabic original diverge, the guide follows the Arabic and records the difference in a note.

Two more narrations appear in the guide on related subjects. ʿĀʾishah’s account of how revelation began, in the cave of Ḥirāʾ, supports the explanation of the first verse of Sūrat al-Qadr.25 Abū Hurayrah’s report that Allah descends to the lowest heaven in the last third of every night underlies the night planner.26 Neither names the Night of Decree, so neither appears in the tables.

How this guide checks its sources

Each hadith passes through the same steps before it is cited. The collection and number are looked up on sunnah.com, which shows the report with its chapter, its reference and, for most collections, a grading. The Arabic and English text is then fetched by number from the hadith-api edition, an open dataset, and compared with the paraphrase the guide intends to use. A report counts as checked only when the two sources agree on the number and the substance.

Two status words record the result. VERIFIED means that the collection, number, wording and grading were matched in live sources on the date shown in the note. NOT_FOUND means that the guide could not match the report at a stated number in the sources it uses. NOT_FOUND describes the state of the guide’s search. It passes no judgement on the report, which may be preserved in a collection the guide has not yet been able to check.

Gradings describe the strength of a report’s chain of transmission, the isnād (إِسْنَاد, “support”), and the soundness of its text, the matn (مَتْن, “text”). Hadith scholars use three main grades, and this guide cites only reports in the first two.27

A grading always belongs to someone. For the collections of al-Bukhārī and Muslim the grading is the judgement of the compiler, accepted by later scholarship. For the other collections this guide names the scholar or the edition that issued the grade, such as al-Albānī or the Dār al-Salām edition, and shows both when they differ. Numbering also depends on the edition. Muslim’s collection is cited in the numbering most widely used today, in which a letter after the number marks one of several chains grouped together, so 762a is the first chain under number 762. Other printings number the same reports differently.

Qurʾānic text follows a stricter rule. It is never typed or recalled from memory. Each verse is fetched from Quran.com in the script of the King Fahd Complex, known as KFGQPC Hafs, and copied exactly as returned. It is then set in the matching typeface and in no other, so that Qurʾānic text and hadith always look different on the page.

Reports this guide holds back

Many statements about Laylat al-Qadr circulate in articles, sermons and messages without a source that can be checked. The table names the most common of them, as they are reported, and gives the reason each one is held back. Holding a report back is a statement about evidence the guide has been able to examine. It does not declare the report false, and any report here will move to the tables above once it has been verified.

The authentic reports already cover what a believer needs for the night: where to seek it, how the Prophet ﷺ spent it, what to say in it, and what reward is promised for it. The guide’s pages on prayer and worship and on the last ten nights are built on those reports alone.

Printed editions

The online texts used on this page reproduce printed editions, and the notes name them. The al-Bukhārī texts follow the Arabic and English edition whose numbering sunnah.com uses.29 The Muslim texts follow the numbering of Muḥammad Fuʾād ʿAbd al-Bāqī.30 The Abū Dāwūd text carries the grading of al-Albānī.31 The al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah texts carry the gradings of al-Albānī.32 The Qurʾānic text is that of the Madinah Muṣḥaf in the reading of Ḥafṣ.33 Collation against the physical volumes is still to be done.34

Common questions

Why does a hadith have different numbers on different websites?

Collections have been printed in several editions, and some count each chain separately while others group parallel chains under one number. This guide gives the number used on sunnah.com and links to the page, so the report can be found whichever edition a reader owns.

Can a weak hadith be used for encouragement?

Scholars have discussed this question at length and do not all answer it the same way. This guide takes the cautious course and cites only reports graded ṣaḥīḥ or ḥasan, because the authentic material on the night is already ample.

How can I report an error?

Each note gives the link and the date of the check. If a link no longer matches, or a grading has changed, the contact page reaches the editor. Corrections are made on the page and recorded with a new date.

Printed edition behind the Qurʾānic text: the Madinah Muṣḥaf in the reading of Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim, printed by the King Fahd Glorious Qurʾān Printing Complex, whose digital text and typeface Quran.com supplies.

The editions above are those reproduced by the online sources this guide checks. They have not yet been collated against the physical volumes; a reader who finds a difference is asked to report it through the contact page.
